title: European jazz musicians as imitators, and the Baden-Baden TV show
summary: European players call themselves imitators of the originators; he describes a blues singer named Barrow and the Vienna guitarist at the Baden-Baden show.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah, he had the best band for many, many years. He had a real good band. And I'll tell you what I would, what I would like to get back to, uh, England again. For him. For, for. For one thing I wanted, I wanted to, you know, the musicians to know that how much these, these musicians over in Europe, not only England, are interested in the New Orleans music. And they actually, they, they have it at heart. And good as they play. Now we met some musicians, they actually play very, I mean they play really good. But they always feel like the New Orleans musicians are the greatest, you see. Because they tell you, they say, well we playing, we imitators and you are the originators. And we, we, we playing what you, what you play. But if you would just hear them play, you would just be saying, oh, these guys here is great, you know. But they, good as they play, they, they always, they feels that, uh, they, the imitators, you're the originators. And they say, well you're great, isn't it? Right. But they, that's the good. They got everything that you can name. They got good trumpet players. They got, uh, they got good clarinet players, trombone players, bass players. And to my surprise, I went in a place that had a Dixeland band there. This fellow was, I have his name in the book. But he had a singer with him. Her name was Barrow. And the place was so crowded, you know, I couldn't see the band when I first went in. And I heard this band playing and this band, you know, sound, oh, just like a New Orleans band, you know. And I say, oh, these guys really can play some music. And whoever it was, man. And then after a while I heard somebody singing the blues, you know, and it sounded like Mamie Smith or one of them. And when I look up there, it was a big blonde. Her name is Barrow. And then she can sing the blues and they got some boys over there who can play the blues just like they played years ago, you know, that real lowdown blues. Them guys can play those blues. I used to, I'd sit down and listen to them, I'd say, now look, these fellas can play these blues, but I wouldn't even think about knowing how to play them. You know, during those times it was for me and all of us used to play the blues was the first thing we was most alone, you know, a routine piano player. And those guys, man, play the blues and play you something, anything you want to play, and they got some progressive men over there too, or they got some of that, they got some of the blues and play everything you can name. And I met a guitar player, he was playing with Oscar Petterford, the bass player. Well in Germany, in Baden-Baden, on this television show, there was a play, you know, where we had been rehearsing, and they kept telling us they had a trio that was going to be on the show with us too, you see. So the last day of rehearsal, these guys came in, you know. But I didn't see them, I didn't see them when they come in because I had went to the canteen. And when I come back I heard a guitar player, I heard a guitar, this is a gun, you know, a guy was playing, and I said, this is a cat and you're playing this guitar, you know. And to George say, yeah man, who's this cat? And when we looked up there, this guy, he was playing and he was a guy, he was from Vienna.
